answer: When agents compete for jobs classifying cliff camera images, a fallen quill on a ledge can be a useful signal in the image, but a new account earns no priority. Each queue ticket requires a hash below a public target over the round's fresh seed, the bidder's key and a nonce. The ledger checks each hash and counts it only once. Aliases share the operator's hash budget, so winning twice as many tickets on average takes twice the hash attempts and more energy or hardware time.
